34932: Midtribulationists believe the church will be taken up halfway through the seven years. The first half is a time of trouble, but the second half is when God's fiercest judgments fall. Believers are rescued before that worst period.
34933: The church faces some hardship but is rescued before the worst judgments.
34934: Like a rescue team that pulls people out midway through the storm, before its fiercest stretch.
34935: The prewrath view says the church will go through much of the final seven years, including a period of intense persecution by the Antichrist. But before God pours out his wrath on the world, Christ will come and gather his people. Persecution from people and wrath from God are different things.
34936: Believers may suffer persecution, but they will be spared God's wrath.
34937: Like being caught in a fight in the street but being pulled out before the police raid begins.
34938: Posttribulationists hold that the rapture and the second coming are one event, after the tribulation. The church will stay faithful through the final troubles, and God will protect it spiritually. When Jesus returns, believers rise to meet him and come back with him.
34939: The church goes through the tribulation and meets Jesus when he comes back.
34940: Like townspeople going out to meet a returning king and escorting him back into the city.
34941: Most Christians in history, including Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and many other churches, read Paul's words about being 'caught up' as describing Jesus' single, final return, not a separate secret event. When Jesus comes, the dead are raised and the living are changed. Then come judgment and the new creation.
34942: There is one return of Christ, and the 'catching up' is part of it.
34943: Like a welcoming crowd running out to greet a returning hero and then walking back with him in one joyful parade.
34944: Dominion theology is a family of ideas saying Christians should bring every area of society under Christ's rule. One stream, called Christian Reconstruction or theonomy, wants Old Testament civil laws applied today; another, charismatic stream speaks of the church influencing 'seven mountains' of culture. Many other Christians, from several traditions, criticise these ideas.
34945: The disagreement is about how, and how far, Christians should seek to shape law, government and culture for Christ.
34946: This shapes how believers engage in politics, business, education and media. It raises questions about religious freedom, power, and what it looks like to love a pluralist society.
34947: Christian Reconstructionists teach that God's law, including the civil laws and penalties of the Old Testament, still applies to every area of life, including government. 'Theonomy' means 'God's law.' They expect society to be transformed gradually as people are converted and choose to live by God's law, not by force.
34948: God's law is the best law for every nation, and Christians should work for it peacefully.
34949: Like a manufacturer's manual: the one who made the machine knows best how it should run.
34950: The charismatic 'Kingdom Now' and 'Seven Mountains' teaching says God's kingdom is present and advancing, and the church is his agent to show his rule everywhere. Christians should bring godly influence to seven key areas of culture: family, religion, education, government, media, arts and business. Its teachers stress influence and service, though they differ on how far this should go.
34951: Christians are called to bring God's goodness into every major sphere of society.
34952: Like a team sending skilled players into every position on the field, not just one.
34953: Critics include Reformed scholars, 'two-kingdoms' theologians (who keep church and state roles distinct), dispensationalists, Anabaptists and supporters of a pluralist society. They argue Christ's kingdom advances mainly through the gospel and the church, not by taking control of political power. Many worry these programmes misread the Old Testament and can threaten freedom of conscience.
34954: Christ's kingdom is not of this world and does not advance by seizing cultural or political control.
34955: Like a doctor who heals by caring for patients one by one, not by taking over the hospital board.
34956: The Word of Faith movement teaches that faith, expressed in confident words, releases God's promises of health, provision and blessing. Its 'prosperity' form emphasises financial blessing. Critics say this misreads the Bible, while a middle group says the movement has real excesses but also real insights.
34957: The debate is about whether God has promised health and wealth to all who believe, and how faith and spoken words work.
34958: This shapes how people pray when sick or poor, how they interpret suffering, and how they give money. It deeply affects churches worldwide, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia.
34959: Word of Faith teachers say God has bound himself to his promises, and faith is how those promises become real in a believer's life. Faith is expressed by speaking God's word confidently, not by speaking doubt. Because of Jesus' work, believers can expect healing and provision as part of God's blessing.
34960: God keeps his promises, and believing faith spoken aloud lays hold of them.
34961: Like cashing a cheque someone has already signed for you: you have to present it in confidence.
34962: Critics, including evangelical, Pentecostal and historical scholars, say the movement departs from the gospel at important points. They argue it treats faith like a force that controls outcomes, promises wealth God never guaranteed, and can blame sick or poor people for 'lack of faith.' They point to Jesus and the apostles, who suffered and lived simply.
34963: Faith trusts God himself, not a formula, and the Christian life includes suffering.
34964: Like confusing a loving father with a vending machine that pays out if you press the right buttons.
34965: A middle group, mostly charismatic writers and historians, admits the movement has produced real excesses but rejects the verdict that it is a 'different gospel.' They argue its roots are in earlier holiness and healing movements, not mainly in fringe religion. They call for correction from within, keeping its emphasis on bold faith while rejecting greed.
34966: Keep the confident faith, fix the excesses.
34967: Like a garden overgrown with weeds that still has good plants worth saving.
34968: Some Christians believe God is restoring apostles and prophets to lead the church today, as part of a movement often called the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR). Others argue this misreads the New Testament and gives leaders too much authority. A third group believes prophecy continues but must be carefully tested and kept accountable.
34969: The question is whether God gives modern apostles and prophets with authority, and how prophecy should be tested.
34970: This shapes church leadership, how people respond to a prophetic word about their lives or nations, and how believers handle predictions that fail. It also affects how churches guard against spiritual abuse.
34971: Supporters believe God has gradually restored truths and ministries to the church since the Reformation, and is now restoring the offices of apostle and prophet. These leaders help equip believers and give direction to the church. They see this as fulfilling Paul's list of gifts that build up the church until it matures.
34972: God is restoring apostles and prophets to equip the church for its mission today.
34973: Like a team rediscovering positions it had forgotten to field, and finally playing at full strength.
34974: Critics argue the movement misreads the New Testament on apostles and prophets, creating leaders who claim a kind of authority that scripture does not give. The original apostles laid a one-time foundation for the church. They warn of failed predictions, lack of accountability and pressure on believers to obey leaders.
34975: The apostles' foundation is finished, and no modern leader should claim their authority.
34976: Like adding new floors to a house is fine, but you cannot pour a second foundation.
34977: A third group believes prophecy and other spiritual gifts continue today but must be used within clear biblical guardrails. Prophecy should be humble, tested by scripture and the church, and never treated as equal to the Bible. Failed predictions should be admitted and corrected openly.
34978: Welcome prophecy, but test everything and hold prophets accountable.
34979: Like a smoke alarm worth having, as long as you check it works and don't panic at every beep.
34980: Jesus healed many people, and Christians still pray for the sick. They disagree about what to expect. Some believe healing is guaranteed by Jesus' death, some expect healing often but not always, and others doubt miraculous healing gifts continue today or warn against false promises.
34981: The debate is about whether God has promised physical healing now, and how to pray when healing does not come.
34982: This shapes how churches pray for the sick, how they comfort those who are not healed, and how they relate faith to medicine. Getting it wrong either way can deeply hurt people.
34983: The healing movement teaches that Jesus' death on the cross paid not only for sin but also for bodily healing. Just as Jesus healed all who came to him, believers today can receive healing by faith. Sickness is seen as part of the curse that Christ came to break.
34984: Healing is part of what Jesus won on the cross, so believers can ask for it with confidence.
34985: Like a bill already paid in full: you simply claim what has been bought for you.
34986: This middle view follows scholar George Eldon Ladd's teaching that God's kingdom has 'already' arrived in Jesus but is 'not yet' complete. So healings really happen today as signs of the kingdom, and Christians should pray with expectation. But full healing awaits Christ's return, so not everyone is healed now.
34987: Pray boldly for healing, but accept that the full cure comes only when Christ returns.
34988: Like a sunrise: real light is already breaking through, but full daylight is still coming.
34989: Critics raise three kinds of objection. Cessationists say the miraculous gift of healing belonged to the apostles' time and has ceased. Others ask for medical evidence of claimed miracles, and still others stress that God often works through suffering and that promising healing can wound those who stay sick.
34990: God can heal, but he has not promised to, and suffering is not proof of weak faith.
34991: Like a father who sometimes says 'no' or 'not yet' because he sees a bigger picture than his child does.
34992: Many Christians speak of God 'telling' them things through impressions, nudges or an inner voice. Others believe God speaks today through the Bible, made clear by the Holy Spirit, and warn against treating feelings as messages. A third view says God does not have a hidden detailed plan we must discover, but gives us wisdom to choose well.
34993: The question is how God guides his people today, and how much to rely on inner impressions.
34994: This shapes how people make big decisions about jobs, marriage and moving, how they pray, and how anxious they feel about 'missing God's will.' It also affects how much authority people give to someone who says 'God told me.'
34995: This view holds that God wants a living, conversational relationship with his people, not just a rulebook. Writer Dallas Willard taught that believers can learn to recognise God's voice in their thoughts, always tested by scripture. God speaks personally, guiding and comforting as a friend would.
34996: God is a friend who still speaks, and we can learn to recognise his voice.
34997: Like learning to recognise a close friend's voice on the phone before they say their name.
34998: Many Reformed Christians hold that God now speaks to his people through the Bible, which the Holy Spirit helps them understand and apply. He does not give new personal revelations alongside it. Impressions and feelings can be useful, but they are not God's voice and should not be treated with that authority.
34999: God's voice is found in his written word, which is all we need to live for him.
35000: Like a complete instruction manual already in your hands: you do not need extra notes slipped under the door.
35001: Garry Friesen's 1980 book Decision Making and the Will of God challenged the idea that God has a hidden, detailed plan for every choice that we must find. Instead, God's moral will is in scripture, and within it we have freedom to choose wisely. We pray, seek counsel and use good judgment, trusting God's control of everything.
35002: Obey what God has said, then make wise choices freely without fearing you missed a secret plan.
35003: Like a parent who sets the house rules and then says 'you choose which of these good options you want.'
35004: In the New Testament, believers sometimes 'spoke in tongues,' praying or praising in languages they had not learned. Christians disagree about what this gift was, whether it continues today, and whether it is the sign that someone has been 'baptized in the Holy Spirit.'
35005: The debate is about what speaking in tongues is and whether every Spirit-filled believer should expect it.
35006: This shapes how churches worship, whether believers seek this gift, and how they view Christians who do or do not speak in tongues. It can be a source of joy and also of division.
35007: Classical Pentecostals teach that 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' is an empowerment for witness, usually after conversion. Its first outward sign, the 'initial evidence,' is speaking in tongues, as happened in the book of Acts. Every believer should seek this experience.
35008: Tongues are the normal first sign that a believer has been filled with the Spirit.
35009: Like the first cry of a newborn baby: a sign that new life has truly arrived.
35010: Charismatic Christians believe the gift of tongues continues and is valuable. It is a way of praying and praising God from the spirit, and it builds up the person praying. But not every believer must speak in tongues to be Spirit-filled, since the Spirit gives different gifts to different people.
35011: Tongues are a good gift to welcome, but not a required badge of the Spirit.
35012: Like players on one team with different skills: some score goals, but everyone is on the team.
35013: Cessationists believe the New Testament gift of tongues was the miraculous ability to speak real human languages the speaker had not learned, as at Pentecost. It served as a sign while the New Testament was being given, and it ended with the apostles. They are cautious about modern experiences that do not match this description.
35014: Biblical tongues were real languages given as a sign for the apostles' time.
35015: Like scaffolding on a new building: essential at the start, then removed once the structure stands.
